items.text: In this lesson you tell the story of your life: where you grew up, what you used to do, and the turning points that changed your life. You read how one town changed after its factory closed down, and you tell your own story for a community history project.

Everyone has a life story, and most life stories have a turning point: a moment when your life went in a new direction. In this lesson, you tell your own story. But first, you listen to Kwame. He's a bus driver, and he's going to retire at the end of the week. At lunch, his colleague Priya asks him about his life. Listen for three useful phrases. When I was younger… I grew up in… That's when I decided to… When Kwame was young, he had a big ambition. Listen for what it was, what happened to it, and who helped him at the time.

Now, the grammar. When we talk about the past, we often use used to. I used to live by the sea. I used to be very shy. It means: this was true for a long time, but it isn't true now. We can also use would, for things we did again and again. Every Saturday, my grandfather would take me to the match. But be careful. Would is only for actions. For states, like be, have, live and like, use used to. So: I used to have long hair. Not: I would have long hair. In questions and negatives, the d disappears. Did you use to work here? I didn't use to like coffee. You also learn three verbs for a life story. You grow up in a place. Someone brings you up. And later, you settle down.

Next, you read an article by Ruth. She grew up in a small town where one factory employed almost everyone. When she was fourteen, the factory closed down. Read it once for the main idea: how did the town change? Then read the form she filled in for a community history project. Look for the words that show then and now: in those days, nowadays, compared with. After that, you write two paragraphs about a place you know. First, what it used to be like. Then, what it's like nowadays.

Then you tell your life story for a community history project. You only have two minutes, so plan it first. Tell it in four parts, in order. Where you grew up. What you used to do. Your turning point. And your life now. Don't write every sentence on paper. Write a few key words, and speak. At the end, say how you feel when you look back. For example: Looking back, I'm glad I left home. Or: Looking back, I'm glad I changed my mind.

Last, you read a longer story about someone's life. Read it once for the story, and look for the turning point. Then read it again and answer the questions. Finally, compare the story with your own life. Was your turning point bigger or smaller?

So, Kwame, only four more days. Are you ready to retire?
I think so. It feels strange, though. I've driven buses here for thirty years.
Did you always want to be a driver?
Not at all. When I was younger, my big ambition was to play football.
Really? Where did you grow up?
I grew up in a small town by the sea. My grandparents brought me up.

Very happy. Every Saturday, my grandfather would take me to watch the local team, and I used to practise on the beach every evening.
So what happened?
When I was eighteen, I hurt my knee badly. At the time, I thought my life was over.
Oh no. What did you do?
My uncle drove buses in the city, and he encouraged me to try it. That's when I decided to leave home.
So that was the turning point.
Exactly. I moved to the city, got married and settled down. Looking back, I wouldn't change a thing.
Thank you for coming in, Carlos. Could you start by telling me where you grew up?
Of course. I grew up in a village near Valencia, in Spain. My mother brought me up on her own.
What was life like in the village?
Very quiet. In the summer I used to help my uncle on his farm, and every evening the whole village would sit outside and talk.
And when did you come here?
In 1998. A friend offered me a job in a restaurant. At the time, I didn't speak any English at all.

It was. But the owner encouraged me to go to evening classes. That was the turning point. My confidence grew, and five years later I became the manager.
And what about your life now?
Nowadays I run a small café on Market Street. I got married and settled down here, and my two children have grown up.
Looking back, would you change anything?
Not really. Well, maybe I'd start learning English earlier!
Thank you, Carlos. That's a wonderful story.

In this lesson you connect the past to now. You talk about how a job has changed, how long you have been doing something, and what you have learned. You read about a furniture maker's twenty years at the same bench, and you tell an old friend how your life has changed.

This lesson is about change: in your job, in your town, and in you. First, you listen to Mei and Omar. They work at a parcel depot. Mei has just started, and Omar has been there for more than fifteen years. Omar says: Things have changed a lot since I started. In those days, we sorted every parcel by hand. Now there are automatic machines, and everything is digital. Listen for how Omar felt about the change, and what he has been doing since his promotion.

Now, the grammar. English has two main ways to talk about the past, and they say different things. The past simple is for a finished time. I started here in 2010. They installed the machines last year. The present perfect connects the past to now. I've worked here for ten years. That means: I still work here. So when you say a finished time, like in 2010 or last year, use the past simple. Then there is the present perfect continuous: have been, and the -ing form of the verb. It's for an activity that started in the past and is still going on. I've been working here since March. How long have you been learning English? A very common mistake is: I am working here since March. Say: I've been working here since March.

Next, you read an article by Samir, a furniture maker. He has worked at the same bench for twenty years, and almost everything about his job has changed. Then you read his training record. It shows the courses he has done this year, and how many hours he still needs. Read the numbers carefully. After that, you write about what has changed in your own job, your studies or your town. Say what it was like when you started, and what it's like now.

Then you meet an old friend in a café. You haven't seen each other for ten years. Your friend asks: What have you been doing? How has the town changed? Tell your story in order. Say what you did before, in the past simple. Say what has changed, in the present perfect. And say how long you have been doing your job now. Finish with one thing you have learned. For example: What I've learned is that change is hard at first, but it gets easier.
Last, you read a longer story or article about change. Read it once for the main idea: what changed, and how did people feel about it? Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you describe people, places and things in detail, so that nobody needs to ask again. You compare two quotes for the same job, and you read a catalogue entry and a returns form. Then you describe a lost bag so precisely that the lost property office finds it first time.

This lesson is about describing things precisely, so that nobody needs to ask again. First, you listen to Nadia and Diego. They run a small café, and they need a new counter. Two firms have sent them quotes. One is cheap, and one is more expensive. Listen for three useful phrases. It's the one that… It's a kind of… What does it look like? Listen for the price, the material and the size of each counter. Then decide: which one is better value for money?

Now, the grammar. To say which one you mean, use who, which, that, where and whose. Who is for people: the woman who found my wallet. Which is for things: the bag which I lost. That is for people or things: the firm that made our counter. Where is for places: the café where we met. And whose is for belonging: the man whose bag was stolen. Then, adjective order. First your opinion, then size, age, shape, colour and material, and last the noun. A lovely small brown leather bag. Two words can also make one adjective: a well-made chair, a hand-made table, a ten-minute walk. With a number, the noun stays singular. Say a ten-minute walk, not a ten-minutes walk.

Next, you read a page from a shop's catalogue. It describes a leather bag and a purse: the size, the weight, the colour, and what's inside. Read the numbers carefully. Then you read a returns form. A customer's new bag arrived with a broken zip and a long scratch. Notice how specific she is. She doesn't just say it's bad. She says what is wrong, and where. After that, you write a description of something you have lost, for a lost property office.

Then you go to the lost property office at a station. You left your bag on a train, and the office has three bags that look almost the same. Describe yours so precisely that they find it first time. Say the size, the colour and the material. Say what's inside. And give one detail that only the owner knows. For example: There's a small scratch on the front, near the zip. Give facts, not opinions. Don't say: It's a nice bag. Say: It's a dark green leather bag with a long strap.

Last, you read a longer story or article. Notice how the writer describes people and places, and which small details make them easy to picture. Read it once for the story, then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you learn to tell a story well: you set the scene, tell the events in order and say how people reacted. You read a worker's account of an accident and the incident report about it. Then you tell a friend about a day you will never forget, and write it up as a short report.

In this lesson, you learn to tell a story well. First, you listen to Tomasz. He works in the delivery yard of a big shop. Yesterday there was an accident at work, and today he tells his friend Amina about it. Listen to how he starts. He doesn't start with the accident. He starts with the scene: It was getting dark, and most people were going home. Then the event arrives: All of a sudden, we heard a loud noise. And at the end, he tells her how it finished: In the end, the manager came and calmed everyone down. Listen to Amina, too. A good listener reacts: Oh no! And then? Was anybody hurt?

A good story uses three past tenses together. The past continuous sets the scene. It was getting dark. People were going home. These things were already happening when the story started. The past simple tells the events, one after another. We heard a noise. The trolley hit the shelves. Two shelves collapsed. We often join the two with when. I was checking the shelves when we heard a noise. The long action is the background. The short action cuts across it. The past perfect goes one step further back. It tells you what had happened before the story started. Somebody had left the trolley at the top of the yard. When we speak, had is short and quiet. I'd forgotten. She'd gone home. But don't use the past perfect for every event. When things happen in order, the past simple is enough: I got up, had a shower and left.

Next, you read two texts about the same accident. The first is Kwame's account for the staff newsletter. He writes it like a story. He tells you about the dark yard, the strange noise and how people felt. The second is the incident report. It gives only the facts: the date, the time, the location, what took place and what was done. Notice the difference. A story makes the reader feel something. A report helps the reader check what happened. Then you write the opening of a story. Set the scene first: where it takes place, when, and what was happening. Then write the moment when everything changes.

In the task, you tell a friend about a day you will never forget. It can be real, or you can invent it. Start with the scene. Then tell the events in order. Say how people reacted, and how it ended. Your friend reacts and asks questions: Oh no! What happened next? Then you write the same story as a short report. This time, no feelings. Just the facts, in order: when, where, what happened, and what was done.

Last, you read a story from the Library. Before you read, look at the title and guess where it takes place. Read it once for the plot: what happens, and to whom. Then read it again and notice how the writer sets the scene.

In this lesson you talk about plans that depend on something, like the weather or the money you have. You make a plan B for an event, read simple hire terms and a repair card, and give a friend advice about their plans.

In this lesson, you make plans that depend on something, and you give advice. First, you listen to Mei. She's organising a leaving party for a colleague, Samir. She wants an outdoor party in the park. But what if it rains? Mei hasn't got a plan B, and she's stressed. Her friend Carlos gives her advice. Listen to how he does it. He doesn't say: Do this. He says: If I were you, I'd book a backup venue. And: You should book it in advance. Listen for three useful phrases: as long as, as soon as, and just to be on the safe side.

There are two grammar points in this lesson. The first is plans that depend on something. If it rains, we'll move to the café. The if half is in the present: if it rains. The other half has will: we'll move. Don't put will in the if half. Say: if it rains. Not: if it will rain. The same is true after unless, as long as and as soon as. I'll ring the café as soon as I get home. Not: as soon as I will get home. Unless means if not. Unless it rains, we'll eat outside. As long as means only if. They won't charge for the room as long as everyone orders food. The second point is advice. You should book early. You ought to warn people. Should and ought to mean the same. Ought needs to after it. Should doesn't. Needn't means it isn't necessary. You needn't buy all the food.

Next, you read two short documents. The first is the terms and conditions of a party hire company. Read the small words carefully: as long as, unless, otherwise. That is where the money is. When are the things due back? What happens if you're late? How do you get your deposit back? The second is a repair card from a community hall. The lift is out of order. The card tells you how to report a fault, and what happens next. Then you write your own plan for an event, and what you'll do if something goes wrong.

In the task, you plan an event: a party, a family day out or a small concert. You have a budget, and you need a plan B. First, tell your partner your plan. Say what you'll do if something goes wrong. Then listen to your partner's plan and give advice. If I were you, I'd … You ought to … You needn't … Good advice is short, clear and kind. And it gives a reason.
Last, you read a story from the Library about a plan that goes wrong. Read it once for the story. Then read it again, and think: what would you advise the people in it?

In this lesson you talk about how things are made and how services work, using the passive. You read a product label, a notice at a warehouse gate and a reply that says nothing, and you write a notice of work that will be done. Then you explain how something from your country is made, and chase up a repair that is late.

In this lesson, you talk about how things are made, and how services work. First, you listen to Ana. She runs a small café, and she's buying aprons for her staff at a workwear shop. She also wants to collect a jacket she left there for repair. Listen to how the assistant, Kwame, talks about the aprons. They're made of cotton. They're made here in our own workshop. He doesn't say who makes them. The aprons are more important than the people. Then listen to the bad news about Ana's jacket: It's still being repaired. And the promise: It'll be finished by Friday.

The grammar in this lesson is the passive. We use it when the thing is more important than the person who does the action, or when we don't know who does it. The passive is be and a past participle. Cotton is grown in Egypt. The aprons are made here. For the past, use was or were. The parcel was delivered yesterday. For something happening now, use being. My jacket is being repaired. For the future, use will be. The aprons will be delivered on Thursday. After must, should and can, use be. The form must be signed. It can't be repaired. Don't forget the small word be. Not: the form must signed. Say: the form must be signed. If the person is important, add by. This chair was made by my grandfather.

Next, you read three short texts. The first is a label from a work jacket. It tells you what the jacket is made of, where it was made, and how to wash it. The second is a notice at a warehouse gate. Notices use the passive a lot. Deliveries are accepted at Gate 2. The road will be inspected. The third is an email reply to a complaint. Every sentence is polite. But look again. It gives no date, no name and no number. It's a reply that says nothing. Then you write a notice of your own. Say what will be done, when, and who to contact.

The task has two parts. First, a colleague asks about something from your country: a food, a drink, a cloth or a craft. Explain how it's made, step by step. First, the tea is washed. Then the mint is added. Then you phone a repair shop. You left something there three weeks ago, and it still isn't ready. Chase it up. Be polite, but don't accept a reply that says nothing. Ask for a date and a name.
Last, you read a story or an article from the Library about how something is made or done. Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again, and notice the steps in the process.

At work, people often call when the person they want is not there. In this lesson you take messages and pass them on: you report what people said, what they asked and what they wanted. You also read a message slip and a short witness statement, and you take a phone message for a colleague.

In this lesson, you pass on messages. It happens every day at work. Someone phones, but the person they want is not there. So you take a message, and later you pass it on. First, you listen to Mei. She works at the front desk of a delivery company. Her colleague Samir comes back from a meeting, and Mei tells him about a phone call. Listen to how she does it. She does not repeat the caller word for word. She says: He said that the delivery would be late. He asked me to tell you. He wanted to know if you could ring him back. Listen for the phone phrases too. It was a bad line, so I asked him to speak up. He couldn't reach you. I'll pass it on.

When you report what someone said, the verb often moves back in time. The caller says: I'm running late. You report: She said that she was running late. Is becomes was. Will becomes would. Can becomes could. Be careful with say and tell. Tell needs a person: she told me. Say does not: she said that. Never say: she said me. Questions change too. The caller asks: Are you free on Monday? You report: She asked if you were free on Monday. The word order is normal again: if you were free, not were you free. For instructions and requests, use told or asked, then a person, then to. He told me to wait. She asked me to ring her back. And for what people want, say: She wants you to call her.

Next, you read two short documents. The first is a message slip. Many offices use slips like this. They are called While you were out. A slip shows who called, when they called, and what they want. The second is a short witness statement. A witness writes down what they saw and heard. Notice how the statement reports people's words: He told me that he had hurt his wrist. I asked him if he wanted an ambulance. Then you write a message for a colleague. Say who called and when, what they said, and what they want your colleague to do.

Then you take a phone message for a colleague. Say that your colleague is out, and offer to take a message. Ask for the caller's name, and ask them to spell it. Write down the number, and read it back to check it. Ask what the message is, and when is a good time to call back. Last, pass the message on. Keep it short and accurate: who called, what they said, and what they want.

Finally, you read a story or an article about messages, and how they can change when people pass them on. Read it once for the main story. Then read it again and answer the questions. Notice every time someone reports what another person said, asked or wanted.

In this lesson you talk about your work, your experience and your skills. You practise a job interview: you answer questions with real examples, and you ask a good question at the end. You also read a job application, and you write a short CV profile and a covering message.

In this lesson, you talk about your work and your skills, and you practise a job interview. First, you listen to Carlos. He works in a small hotel, and he wants a better job. He has an interview for the position of front office supervisor. Listen to the questions. The interviewer says: Tell me about a time when you had to work under pressure. This question wants a real example, not an opinion. So Carlos tells a short story: what happened, what he did, and the result. Listen to how he talks about his job: I was responsible for training new staff. I'm in charge of the weekend team. At the end, the interviewer asks: Do you have any questions for us? Carlos has a good question ready. Always have one.

There are two grammar points in this lesson. The first is about small words like for, to and of. We say: the company I worked for. The manager I reported to. The small word goes at the end, and we don't need who or which. Two phrases are very useful at work: responsible for, and in charge of. I was responsible for the stockroom. She's in charge of a team of six. After for and of, use a noun or an -ing word: responsible for training new staff. The second point is about numbers. Interviewers remember numbers, so say how big the difference was. We had twice as many customers as last year. We had half as many complaints. It was by far the busiest week of the year.

Next, you read a job application. Amina works in customer service, and she wants to be a team leader. Look at the parts: her profile, her experience, her education and her covering letter. Her profile is short, and it has numbers in it. She doesn't just say: I'm hard-working. She says what she does, and what she has achieved. Then you write your own short CV profile, and a covering message for a job you would like.

Then you have a job interview. The interviewer asks you three questions. Answer each one with a real example. Say what the situation was, what you did, and what the result was. Use a number if you can. At the end, ask one good question about the job. For example: What would you like the new person to achieve in the first three months?

Finally, you read a story or an article about work and careers. Read it once for the main story. Then read it again and answer the questions. Think about what the people in it are good at, and what they learn.

In this lesson you give your opinion, and you agree and disagree politely at a residents' meeting. You read the minutes of the meeting and a complaint letter that nobody answered. Then you write a better letter, with four clear points.

In this lesson, you disagree politely, and you give your reasons. First, you listen to a residents' meeting in a block of flats called Priory Court. The residents are deciding how to spend some money. The chair, Grace, proposes cameras at the front entrance. Not everyone agrees. Listen to how people disagree without being rude. Omar says: I see your point, but is that really our biggest issue? Lena says: I'm not sure I agree. And Grace answers: That's true. However, two bikes were stolen. Notice that nobody says: You're wrong. First, they show that they understand. Then they give a different view, and a reason.

There are two grammar points in this lesson. The first is how to join two different ideas. Although joins them in one sentence: Although the cameras are useful, they are expensive. However starts a new sentence: The cameras are useful. However, they are expensive. Put a full stop before however, and a comma after it. While compares two things: While Lena wants a lock, Grace wants cameras. The second point is how to make what you say softer. Use may, might and could. They might cost more than we think. That may not be the best idea. We could put a light on the bike store. These small words make you sound polite, and people listen to you more.

Next, you read two documents. The first is the minutes of the meeting. Minutes are a short written record of what people said and decided. The second is a letter that a resident sent to the council. Nobody replied to it. Read it, and think about why. Look at the tone. Is it polite? Is it clear what he wants? Then you write a better letter. Say what you want at the start. Give four clear points: firstly, secondly, thirdly and lastly. And keep the tone polite.

Then you go to a residents' meeting yourself. The chair proposes a new rule, and you don't agree with it. First, show that you understand: I see your point. Then give your reason. Then suggest a different idea: We could do this instead. For example: I see your point, but many people get home late from work. We could keep the garden open until ten, and ask people to be quiet after nine. Stay calm and polite. You might not win the vote, but people will respect you.

Finally, you read a story or an article about people who disagree. Read it once for the main story. Then read it again and answer the questions. Think about each person's point of view. Who do you agree with, and why?
Your neighbours want to change something in your building, and you don't agree. What do you do?

In this lesson, a plan at work goes wrong, and you help to sort it out without falling out with anyone. You use everyday phrasal verbs like put off, look into and sort out, and you learn when a verb takes -ing and when it takes to. You also read an email that had to be written twice, then write a clear email of your own.

This lesson is about getting along with people when plans change. At work, things come up all the time. A trainer is ill. A delivery doesn't turn up. Somebody is held up in traffic. In the conversation, Lena rings her manager, Samir. Something has come up, and they need to move Friday's training day. Listen for three useful phrases. Can you look into it? We need to put it off. I'm looking forward to it. You will hear a lot of phrasal verbs. A phrasal verb is a verb with a small word after it, like fit in or catch up. The meaning is often not in the two words, so learn each one as a new word. Listen to the stress, too. In a phrasal verb, the small word is strong. Hold up. Sort it out.

There are two grammar points in this lesson. First, some verbs take -ing after them, and some take to. I don't mind waiting. We decided to wait. A few verbs take both, but the meaning changes. Listen. I stopped to eat. That means I stopped work so that I could eat. I stopped eating meat. That means I don't eat meat any more. Remember to call Samir means the call is still to come. I remember calling Samir means I did it, and I have the memory. After looking forward to, always use -ing. I'm looking forward to seeing you. Second, phrasal verbs with the word it. You can say put off the meeting, or put the meeting off. But with it, the small word goes last. Put it off. Never put off it. Look into is different. It never splits. Look into it.

In Section 3 you read two emails from Amina, an office manager. She had to write the same email twice. In the first one, she wrote that a visit was put off. But it was called off. Put off means it will happen later. Called off means it will not happen at all. One small word, and people waited for a new date that was never coming. Read both emails, and find what changed. Then you write your own email with three numbered points. Keep it brief. Give it a clear subject line, and finish with Kind regards.

In the real-life task, you sort out a problem by phone and by email. First, you ring and explain. I'm sorry, but something has come up. Would it be possible to put our meeting off? Then you agree a new time. Would Thursday be convenient? Could you fit me in on Friday? Say the new time back to check it. Last, you follow up the call with an email, so everybody has the new time in writing. Be polite and clear. Say sorry once, then give the new plan.

Last, you read a longer story or article about people who have to get along. Read it once for the story. Who gets on well? Who falls out, and who lets somebody down? Then read it again, and answer the questions.

In this lesson, something goes wrong at work, and people try to work out why. You guess what happened with must have and might have, talk about regrets with should have, and talk about things that are not true with if and I wish. You also read a fair account of a problem, and write one of your own.

This lesson is about things that go wrong, and how we talk about them. When something goes wrong, we look for clues. Then we guess what happened. In the conversation, Mei and Kwame find the café's freezer switched off. All the food in it is soft. The plug is on the floor. Mei says: It must have been the new cleaner. Kwame says: Let's not blame anyone yet. Listen for three phrases. It must have been… If I were you… I should have… Listen to how quickly people say them. Should have sounds like should-uv. Must have sounds like must-uv. But when you write, always write have.

There are two grammar points. The first is about things that are not true now. If I had more time, I'd check everything twice. But I don't have more time. The verb is past, but the meaning is now. To give advice, say: If I were you, I'd ring them today. To say you want something to be different, use I wish and a past verb. I wish I knew what happened. I don't know. The second point is about guessing the past. Must have means you are almost sure. It must have been the cleaners. Can't have means you are almost sure it didn't happen. Might have means perhaps. Should have is for regrets. I should have checked it. I didn't check it, and that was a mistake.

In Section 3 you read a short review. Kwame, the kitchen manager, explains what went wrong with the freezer. He doesn't point the finger at one person. He finds a series of small problems: a lack of communication, no written procedure, and an alarm that wasn't working properly. That is a fair account. It explains what happened, without blaming people unfairly. Then you write two things. First, six wishes about your own life. Then a short, fair account of something that went wrong.

In the real-life task, you talk to a friend about something that went wrong for you. Say what happened. Then say the likely cause. It must have happened at security. Say what you should have done. I should have checked the gate earlier. Last, say what you would do differently. If it happened again, I'd go straight to the gate. Be honest, but be fair to yourself too. Everybody makes mistakes.

Last, you read a longer story or article in which something goes wrong. As you read, look for the clues. Can you work out what happened before the end? Then answer the questions, and say what the people should have done.

In this lesson, something you bought is faulty, and you complain until you get a result. You say what other people did for you with have or get something done, and you read the small print before you buy. This lesson ends the nine-month course, so you also make a plan for learning English on your own.

This is the last lesson of Level 3, and the end of the nine-month course. It is about money, services and complaints. In the conversation, Omar phones a shop. His washing machine is faulty. He had it repaired, but now it's leaking again. Listen to how he complains. He is polite, but he is firm. I'd like to make a complaint. I'd like a refund. The shop says no to a refund, because it's more than fourteen days since he bought it. So Omar asks for something else. Listen for what he gets in the end. A good complaint is clear. Say what you bought, what went wrong, and what you want.

There are two grammar points. First, have or get something done. Omar did not repair the machine himself. The engineer did. So he says: I had it repaired. Have, then the thing, then a past participle. Listen to the difference. I repaired my car means I did the work. I had my car repaired means a mechanic did it. Get is the same, but more informal. I need to get my hair cut. Second, a pattern for two things that change together. The more you order, the lower the price. The sooner you complain, the better. Remember to say the in both halves.

In Section 3 you read two short texts. The first is the small print from a shop: its rules for returns and repairs. Read it carefully. The numbers are important. How many days? How much? The second is Priya's learning plan for the six months after her course. Then you write two things. First, a complaint email: what you bought, what went wrong, what you had done, and what you want. Then your own learning plan.

The real-life task has two parts. First, you phone a shop about headphones that have stopped working again. Don't stop at the first no. Stay polite, say clearly what you want, and ask for it in writing. Then you present your plan for learning after the course. Say your main aim. Then say your habit: a fixed time and place, not a number of hours. Twenty minutes on the bus every morning is better than an hour when you have time. The nine-month course ends here, but your English doesn't. Keep going.

Last, you read a longer story or article about money and services. Read it once for the story. Did the people get a good result? What would you do in their place? Then answer the questions, and tell Wehel about a time you complained.
